lesson.title: Sizing the Cushion: From Standard Error to Margin of Error
lesson.summary: The margin of error scales the standard error by a critical value tied to the desired confidence level, producing the exact cushion added and subtracted from a point estimate.
lesson.body:
The standard error measures typical sampling variability, but on its own it does not say how wide an interval estimate should be. That job belongs to the margin of error, which is defined as a critical value multiplied by the standard error. The critical value, often written z-star for normal based intervals, controls how many standard errors of cushion to build in, and it is chosen based on how confident you want to be that the interval captures the true parameter. The full mechanics of choosing a critical value are covered in a later chapter, but the standard values used throughout this course are 1.645 for 90% confidence, 1.96 for 95% confidence, and 2.576 for 99% confidence.

The reason margin of error multiplies rather than just using the standard error directly is that standard error alone only guarantees capturing the parameter a modest fraction of the time. Multiplying by a critical value stretches the cushion out far enough to reach a chosen, explicitly stated level of confidence. The larger the critical value, which corresponds to demanding higher confidence, the wider the resulting margin of error, and the more room the eventual interval has to actually contain the true parameter.

For the transit survey, the standard error was computed as about 0.0217, from p-hat equals 0.25, n equals 400. At 95% confidence, the critical value is 1.96, so the margin of error is 1.96 times 0.0217, which equals approximately 0.0425. This means the eventual confidence interval will extend about 0.0425, or 4.25 percentage points, above and below the point estimate of 0.25. At 90% confidence, using critical value 1.645, the margin of error shrinks to 1.645 times 0.0217, or about 0.0357. At 99% confidence, using critical value 2.576, it grows to 2.576 times 0.0217, or about 0.0559. Notice the pattern: demanding more confidence always widens the margin of error, because the interval has to work harder to guarantee capturing the parameter that often.

For the bottling example, the standard error of the sample mean was about 1.4142 milliliters, from sigma equals 10, n equals 50. At 95% confidence, the margin of error is 1.96 times 1.4142, which equals approximately 2.77 milliliters. That is the exact cushion the next chapter will add to and subtract from the sample mean of 500 milliliters to build a complete confidence interval.
